claim: Pyrococcus furiosus cells grown in rich medium measure approximately 1-2 μm across.
source: Initial cryoEM showed that P. furiosus cells grown in rich medium, measure ~1–2 μm across (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B showing microscopy images of cells.

claim: Pyrococcus furiosus cells grown in rich medium are too thick and too dense for electron cryo-tomography.
source: Initial cryoEM showed that P. furiosus cells grown in rich medium, measure ~1–2 μm across (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B) and are thus too thick and too dense for electron cryo-tomography.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a conclusion from the cryoEM observations.

claim: Cultivating Pyrococcus furiosus on minimal SME pyruvate medium reduces cell size to 500-1000 nm.
source: By cultivating P. furiosus on minimal SME pyruvate medium, the cell size was reduced to 500–1000 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: In roughly 80% of Pyrococcus furiosus cells, a bundle of up to 50 archaella protrudes from a bulge at the cell pole.
source: In roughly 80% of the cells, a bundle of up to 50 archaella protrudes from a bulge at the cell pole (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1A,B showing tomograms of cells.

claim: Pyrococcus furiosus archaellar filaments have a constant diameter of approximately 11 nm.
source: P. furiosus archaellar filaments have a constant diameter of ~11 nm but vary considerably in length (a few 100 nm to several µm).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text based on tomographic observations.

claim: Pyrococcus furiosus archaellar filaments vary considerably in length from a few hundred nm to several μm.
source: P. furiosus archaellar filaments have a constant diameter of ~11 nm but vary considerably in length (a few 100 nm to several µm).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text based on tomographic observations.

claim: Each Pyrococcus furiosus archaellar filament crosses the S-layer and spans the approximately 34 nm periplasmic gap.
source: Each filament crosses the S-layer and spans the ~34 nm periplasmic gap (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Pyrococcus furiosus archaella traverse the periplasm at variable angles of 60-90° between the filament axis and the membrane plane.
source: As observed previously (Briegel et al., 2017), the archaella traverse the periplasm at variable angles of 60–90° between the filament axis and the membrane plane (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text, supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and cites previous work.

claim: In tomograms, Pyrococcus furiosus archaella emerge from a basal density on the cytoplasmic surface of the plasma membrane, which most likely corresponds to the archaellar motor.
source: In the tomograms, the filaments emerge from a basal density on the cytoplasmic surface of the plasma membrane, which most likely corresponds to the archaellar motor (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text with an inference about the identity of the density, supported by Figure 1B.

claim: Each archaellar motor density in Pyrococcus furiosus is located in an approximately 35 nm gap between the membrane and a sheet-like cytoplasmic structure called the polar cap.
source: Each of these densities is located in a ~35 nm gap between the membrane and a sheet-like cytoplasmic structure (polar cap; Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1A,B.

claim: The polar cap is a hallmark of motile Euryarchaeota.
source: The polar cap appears to be a hallmark of motile Euryarchaeota, as it has also been observed in related species (Briegel et al., 2017; Kupper et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The polar cap has a thickness of approximately 3 nm.
source: The polar cap has a thickness of ~3 nm, a variable diameter of 200–600 nm and typically straight edges.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text based on tomographic observations.

claim: The polar cap has a variable diameter of 200-600 nm.
source: The polar cap has a thickness of ~3 nm, a variable diameter of 200–600 nm and typically straight edges.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text based on tomographic observations.

claim: The polar cap was observed in all Pyrococcus furiosus cells in which archaella were present and never in the absence of an archaellar bundle.
source: We observed the polar cap in all cells in which archaella were present and never in the absence of an archaellar bundle (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 1C showing quantification.

claim: Six-fold symmetry was applied during sub-tomogram averaging of the archaellar motor complex.
source: To analyse the in situ structure of the archaellar motor complex, we performed sub-tomogram averaging of 379 densities at the base of archaellar filaments. Six-fold symmetry was applied during averaging, as the S. acidocaldarius homolog of the central core protein FlaI has been shown to be a hexamer (Reindl et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and justified by citation to previous work.

claim: Purified Pyrococcus furiosus FlaI forms hexameric ring structures as shown by negative stain EM and 2D classification.
source: To validate this assumption for P. furiosus, we overexpressed PfuFlaI in E. coli, purified the protein, recorded negative stain images and performed 2D classification of 130.000 particles, which indeed indicated a hexameric ring structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sub-tomogram average of the Pyrococcus furiosus motor assembly reveals a bell-shaped central density projecting 19 nm from the plasma membrane into the cytosol.
source: The sub-tomogram average of the motor assembly reveals a bell-shaped central density projecting 19 nm from the plasma membrane into the cytosol (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 2A,B.

claim: Proximal to the membrane, the Pyrococcus furiosus motor complex has its narrowest diameter of 9.5 nm.
source: Proximal to the membrane, the complex has its narrowest diameter of 9.5 nm, and is linked to the bilayer via six ~3 nm protrusions (Figure 2A, arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 2A.

claim: The Pyrococcus furiosus motor complex is linked to the bilayer via six approximately 3 nm protrusions.
source: Proximal to the membrane, the complex has its narrowest diameter of 9.5 nm, and is linked to the bilayer via six ~3 nm protrusions (Figure 2A, arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Distal to the membrane, the Pyrococcus furiosus motor complex widens to a diameter of 18 nm and is connected to a cytosolic ring of 26 nm in cross-section.
source: Distal to the membrane, the complex widens to a diameter of 18 nm and is connected to a cytosolic ring of 26 nm in cross-section (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 2A–D.

claim: The periplasmic protein FlaF has been suggested to integrate the archaellum filament into the S-layer.
source: The periplasmic protein FlaF has been suggested to integrate the archaellum filament into the S-layer (Banerjee et al., 2015), however it is not certain that this protein forms a bona fide conduit through the periplasm.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The filament and motor assembly are not structurally aligned with the S-layer in Pyrococcus furiosus.
source: Although the central motor complex is well resolved, both the filament and the regular S-layer structure were averaged out (Figure 2A). This indicates that the filament and motor assembly are not structurally aligned with the S-layer, consistent with the variable angle at which the archaellum crosses the periplasm (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as an inference from the averaging results.

claim: The Pyrococcus furiosus S-layer has a dense protein array of symmetry P1 with lattice parameters of a = 19 nm and b = 17 nm, including an angle of 63.5°.
source: The resulting map (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1) shows a dense protein array of symmetry P1 and lattice parameters of a = 19 nm and b = 17 nm, including an angle of 63.5°.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to figures showing the S-layer structure.

claim: The Pyrococcus furiosus S-layer parameters are inconsistent with the P6 symmetry that has been deduced from freeze-etched cells before.
source: Note that these parameters are inconsistent with the P6 symmetry that has been deduced from freeze-etched P. furiosus cells before (König et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and cites previous work for comparison.

claim: The Pyrococcus furiosus S-layer has narrow, irregular gaps with a maximum width of 3.5 nm.
source: In contrast to the large pores that are often found in S-layers of other archaeal species (Engelhardt, 2007; Veith et al., 2009), the P. furiosus S-layer has narrow, irregular gaps with a maximum width of 3.5 nm.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and contrasted with other species via citations.

claim: The gaps in the Pyrococcus furiosus S-layer are too narrow to accommodate the approximately 11 nm archaellum filament.
source: These gaps are evidently too narrow to accommodate the ~11 nm filament, indicating that the S-layer itself does not form a specific guiding scaffold for the archaellum and suggesting that individual S-layer subunits would need to be locally disassembled for the archaellum to pass through.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as an inference from the structural data.

claim: Removal of a single S-layer subunit would generate sufficient space for the Pyrococcus furiosus archaellum to pass through.
source: Comparing the S-layer structure to the filament width in silico, we found that removal of a single S-layer subunit would generate sufficient space for the archaellum (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 3C showing the comparison.

claim: The central core of the archaeal motor assembly consists of a complex of the membrane-integral platform protein FlaJ and the soluble, cytosolic ATPase FlaI.
source: Previous work has established that the central core of the archaeal motor assembly consists of a complex of the membrane-integral platform protein FlaJ and the soluble, cytosolic ATPase FlaI (Reindl et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: FlaJ is almost completely buried in the lipid bilayer.
source: FlaJ is almost completely buried in the lipid bilayer (Reindl et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The X-ray structure of Sulfolobus acidocaldarius FlaI fits into the membrane-proximal cytosolic part of the Pyrococcus furiosus motor sub-tomogram average.
source: However, a superposition of the X-ray structure of the highly conserved S. acidocaldarius FlaI (SacFlaI; PDB-4IHQ) with the membrane-proximal cytosolic part of the sub-tomogram average places the X-ray structure into a density that closely matches its outline.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the fitting procedure.

claim: Docking Sulfolobus acidocaldarius FlaI into the Pyrococcus furiosus motor average places the six N-terminal domains of FlaI into the six bridging densities between the central complex and the membrane.
source: Docking SacFlaI into this position also places the six N-terminal domains of FlaI into the six bridging densities between the central complex and the membrane (Figure 2A,E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 2A,E.

claim: FlaI interacts with FlaH that most likely forms hexameric rings.
source: According to recently published in vitro binding experiments, FlaI also interacts with FlaH that most likely forms hexameric rings (Chaudhury et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A 6-fold symmetric model of Sulfolobus acidocaldarius FlaH docks adjacent to FlaI in the Pyrococcus furiosus motor average.
source: We thus generated a 6-fold symmetric model of the homologous S. acidocaldarius FlaH (SacFlaH; PDB-4YDS) and docked it directly adjacent to SacFlaI (Figure 2E,F). This superimposes SacFlaH with a second rounded density that has the dimensions of the hexamer.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 2E,F.

claim: The remaining cytosolic subunits FlaC and FlaD/E are most likely located in the unassigned densities of the motor average, especially in the ring region.
source: After docking FlaI and FlaH into our sub-tomogram averaging map, a large portion of the motor average remains unassigned, especially in its ring region (Figure 2E,F). These densities are most likely occupied by the remaining cytosolic subunits FlaC and FlaD/E encoded in the P. furiosus fla-operon.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as an inference from the remaining densities.

claim: All motor assemblies in Pyrococcus furiosus co-localise with the polar cap.
source: By repositioning the motor assembly averages into tomographic volumes, we visualise their positions and mutual arrangement in whole P. furiosus cells (Figure 4A,B). Strikingly, all motor assemblies co-localise with the polar cap, and they are not observed outside this region (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 4A,B.

claim: Motor assemblies in Pyrococcus furiosus are not observed outside the polar cap region.
source: Strikingly, all motor assemblies co-localise with the polar cap, and they are not observed outside this region (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Patches of approximately 9.5 nm hexagonal particles project approximately 15 nm from the intracellular face of the polar cap.
source: Close inspection of the polar cap revealed patches of ~9.5 nm hexagonal particles projecting ~15 nm from its intracellular face (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 4C,D.

claim: Sub-tomogram averaging shows that hexagonal particles associated with the polar cap have a sandwich-like structure and assemble into hexagonal arrays.
source: Sub-tomogram averaging of 57 units shows that these particles have a sandwich-like structure and assemble into hexagonal arrays (Figure 4C,D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), with a centre-to-centre distance between closest neighbours of 14 nm.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to figures showing the averaging results.

claim: The centre-to-centre distance between closest neighbours in the hexagonal protein array is 14 nm.
source: Sub-tomogram averaging of 57 units shows that these particles have a sandwich-like structure and assemble into hexagonal arrays (Figure 4C,D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), with a centre-to-centre distance between closest neighbours of 14 nm.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text based on sub-tomogram averaging.

claim: The Pyrococcus furiosus archaellum map has an overall resolution of 4.2 Å.
source: In order to determine the structure of the P. furiosus archaellar filament, we collected 297 dose-fractionated movies of isolated fibres and calculated a 3D map using helical reconstruction in Relion 2 (Kimanius et al., 2016; He and Scheres, 2017). The resulting map has an overall resolution of 4.2 Å (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Pyrococcus furiosus archaellum has a helical rise of 5.41 Å and a rotation of 108.03°.
source: The resulting map has an overall resolution of 4.2 Å (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and reveals a 110 Å-wide helix with a helical rise of 5.41 Å and a rotation of 108.03° (Figure 5A–C, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to figures and Table 1.

claim: The Pyrococcus furiosus archaellum is 110 Å wide.
source: The resulting map has an overall resolution of 4.2 Å (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and reveals a 110 Å-wide helix with a helical rise of 5.41 Å and a rotation of 108.03° (Figure 5A–C, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to figures and Table 1.

claim: The backbone of the Pyrococcus furiosus archaellum is formed by a bundle of α-helices, surrounded by an outer layer rich in β-strands.
source: The backbone of the archaellum is formed by a bundle of α-helices, surrounded by an outer layer rich in β-strands (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 5B.

claim: The repeating unit of the Pyrococcus furiosus archaellum helical array is a lollipop-shaped protein with an extended inward-facing α-helix and an outward-facing globular domain of several ß-strands.
source: The repeating unit of the helical array is a lollipop-shaped protein with an extended inward-facing α-helix and an outward-facing globular domain of several ß-strands (Figure 5B)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 5B.

claim: An atomic model could be built based on the FlaB0 sequence but not on FlaB1 or FlaB2.
source: To investigate which of the three FlaB proteins constitute the P. furiosus archaellum, we attempted to build atomic models of FlaB0, FlaB1 and FlaB2, using their respective sequences. Guided by large resolved side chains (Figure 5D and E) and the structure of the M. hungatei homolog (Poweleit et al., 2016) as a reference, we were able to build a model based on the FlaB0 sequence (Table 1), but not on FlaB1 or FlaB2.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the model building process.

claim: The density map of the Pyrococcus furiosus archaellum fitted FlaB0 well but could not be reconciled with the inserts found in FlaB1 or FlaB2.
source: Whilst our density map fitted FlaB0 well, it could not be reconciled with the inserts found in FlaB1 or FlaB2 (Figure 5—figure supplements 3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplements 3.

claim: At least the main part of the Pyrococcus furiosus archaellum filament is composed of FlaB0 rather than a combination of all three FlaB proteins.
source: This suggests that at least the main part of the filament is composed of FlaB0 rather than a combination of all three FlaB proteins, in accordance with previous biochemical data that identified FlaB0 as the major archaellin of P. furiosus (Näther-Schindler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as an inference from the modeling results and supported by citation.

claim: The density map allowed the FlaB0 polypeptide to be modelled from Ala6 onwards.
source: Our density map allowed the FlaB0 polypeptide to be modelled from Ala6 onwards, in accordance with posttranslational removal of the short, positively charged N-terminal MAKKG peptide prior to FlaB0 filament assembly.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the model.

claim: The short, positively charged N-terminal MAKKG peptide is removed posttranslationally prior to FlaB0 filament assembly.
source: Our density map allowed the FlaB0 polypeptide to be modelled from Ala6 onwards, in accordance with posttranslational removal of the short, positively charged N-terminal MAKKG peptide prior to FlaB0 filament assembly.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as an inference from the modeling results.

claim: The signal peptide of FlaB0 fits the archaeal consensus cleavage site for class III signal peptides [KRDE][GA][ALIFQMVED][ILMVTAS].
source: This signal peptide fits the archaeal consensus cleavage site for class III signal peptides [KRDE][GA][ALIFQMVED][ILMVTAS] (Esquivel et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The structure of the FlaB0 monomer consists of an N-terminal α-helix of 47 amino acids (A6 – A52).
source: The structure of the FlaB0 monomer consists of an N-terminal α-helix of 47 amino acids (A6 – A52).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the structure.

claim: The first 25 amino acids of the FlaB0 N-terminal helix (A6 – I30) are hydrophobic.
source: The first 25 amino acids of the helix (A6 – I30) are hydrophobic, whereas the second half (Q31 – A52) contains predominantly polar residues and is therefore highly hydrophilic (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 5H.

claim: The second half of the FlaB0 N-terminal helix (Q31 – A52) contains predominantly polar residues and is highly hydrophilic.
source: The first 25 amino acids of the helix (A6 – I30) are hydrophobic, whereas the second half (Q31 – A52) contains predominantly polar residues and is therefore highly hydrophilic (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 5H.

claim: The TMHMM server predicts most of the hydrophobic section of FlaB0 (V7-L29) as trans-membrane.
source: The TMHMM server predicts most of the hydrophobic sections (V7-L29) as trans-membrane, and the subsequent hydrophilic part of the polypeptide as outward-facing (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: In the monomeric, extra-filamentous form of FlaB0, V7-L29 may act as a transmembrane helix.
source: This suggests that in the monomeric, extra-filamentous form of FlaB0, V7-L29 may act as a transmembrane helix, while the remaining domains protrude into the periplasm.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as an inference from the TMHMM prediction.

claim: The major part of the FlaB0 polypeptide (S53 - Q212) contains 15 β-strands that fold into a twisted β-barrel.
source: The major part of the polypeptide (S53 - Q212) contains 15 β-strands that fold into a twisted β-barrel (Figure 6D) with a hydrophobic interior (Figure 5D,H).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to figures.

claim: The β-barrel of FlaB0 has a hydrophobic interior.
source: The major part of the polypeptide (S53 - Q212) contains 15 β-strands that fold into a twisted β-barrel (Figure 6D) with a hydrophobic interior (Figure 5D,H).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to figures.

claim: Upon integration into the filament, the apolar N-terminal α-helix section of FlaB0 establishes hydrophobic interactions with six of its neighbours.
source: Upon integration into the filament, individual FlaB0 subunits interact with one another in multiple ways. The apolar N-terminal α-helix section establishes hydrophobic interactions with six of its neighbours.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the filament structure.

claim: The α-helix bundle formed by FlaB0 N-terminal helices is buried inside the filament and forms its backbone.
source: The resulting α-helix bundle is buried inside the filament and forms its backbone (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 5H,I.

claim: The α-helices in the Pyrococcus furiosus archaellum are arranged at an angle of approximately 15° to the long axis of the archaellum.
source: As the α-helices are arranged at an angle of ~15° to the long axis of the archaellum, their hydrophilic C-terminal sections are close to the periphery, where they contact neighbouring α-helices and β-strands via hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions (Figure 5H–I).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 5H–I.

claim: In the outer sheath of the Pyrococcus furiosus archaellum, each β-barrel interacts with six surrounding neighbours, mainly by hydrophilic contacts.
source: In the outer sheath of the archaellum, each β-barrel interacts with six surrounding neighbours, mainly by hydrophilic contacts (Figure 5H–I).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 5H–I.

claim: The amphipathic character of FlaB0 provides the driving force for filament assembly, in which hydrophobic domains are buried in the centre and hydrophilic surfaces exposed to the surrounding medium.
source: Similar to bacterial T4P-like filaments, (Giltner et al., 2012; Pelicic, 2008), the amphipathic character of FlaB0 would provide the driving force for filament assembly, in which hydrophobic domains are buried in the centre and hydrophilic surfaces exposed to the surrounding medium.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to previous work on similar systems.

claim: Archaellin monomers from denatured archaella can spontaneously reassemble into filamentous structures.
source: In line with this, it has been shown that archaellin monomers from denatured archaella can spontaneously reassemble into filamentous structures (Näther-Schindler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Pyrococcus furiosus FlaB0, Methanospirillum hungatei FlaB3, and Ignicoccus hospitalis Iho670 are structurally conserved in the N-terminal helix.
source: Comparing the structure of the P. furiosus archaellum with that of the Methanospirillum hungatei archaellum (Poweleit et al., 2016) as well as the adhesion fibre from the immotile Ignicoccus hospitalis (Braun et al., 2016; Müller et al., 2009) (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A,B), highlights different degrees of domain-specific conservation. Both archaellins (P. furiosus PfuFlaB0 and M. hungatei MhuFlaB3), as well as the I. hospitalis (Iho670) fibre subunit are structurally conserved in the N-terminal helix (Figure 5—figure supplements 6)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to figures and citations.

claim: Pyrococcus furiosus FlaB0, Methanospirillum hungatei FlaB3, and Ignicoccus hospitalis Iho670 show the same amphipathic character.
source: In addition, the three proteins show the same amphipathic character (Figure 5—figure supplement 5E)
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 5E.

claim: Pyrococcus furiosus FlaB0, Methanospirillum hungatei FlaB3, and Ignicoccus hospitalis Iho670 assemble into filaments that have similar helical parameters but distinct diameters.
source: In addition, the three proteins show the same amphipathic character (Figure 5—figure supplement 5E) and assemble into filaments that have similar helical parameters but distinct diameters (100 Å for M. hungatei, 110 Å for P. furiosus and 158 Å for I hospitalis; Figure 5—figure supplement 5 and A,B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to figures.

claim: The Methanospirillum hungatei archaellum has a diameter of 100 Å.
source: and assemble into filaments that have similar helical parameters but distinct diameters (100 Å for M. hungatei, 110 Å for P. furiosus and 158 Å for I hospitalis; Figure 5—figure supplement 5 and A,B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to figures.

claim: The Ignicoccus hospitalis Iho670 filament has a diameter of 158 Å.
source: and assemble into filaments that have similar helical parameters but distinct diameters (100 Å for M. hungatei, 110 Å for P. furiosus and 158 Å for I hospitalis; Figure 5—figure supplement 5 and A,B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to figures.

claim: Differences in filament thickness between Pyrococcus furiosus, Methanospirillum hungatei, and Ignicoccus hospitalis are due to insertions and deletions in the C-terminal beta strand-rich domains.
source: These differences in filament thickness are due to insertions and deletions in the C-terminal beta strand-rich domains of PfuFlaB0, MhuFlaB3 and Iho670 (Figure 5—figure supplements 6), which most likely reflect functional and environmental adaptations in the three species.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplements 6.

claim: Large, irregular, outward-facing densities were found adjacent to five out of 13 asparagine residues (N67, N90, N98, N122 and N128) in FlaB0.
source: While building the atomic FlaB0 model, we found large, irregular, outward-facing densities adjacent to five out of 13 asparagine residues (N67, N90, N98, N122 and N128) (Figure 6A), which were not attributable to the polypeptide backbone or nearby sidechains.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 6A.

claim: The five asparagine residues with adjacent densities (N67, N90, N98, N122 and N128) in FlaB0 are all within a N-X-S/T sequon.
source: Analysis of the FlaB0 sequence revealed that these five amino acids were all within a N-X-S/T sequon (Figure 6F), a highly conserved consensus sequence for N-linked glycosylation (Jarrell et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to Figure 6F and citation.

claim: The N-X-S/T sequon is a highly conserved consensus sequence for N-linked glycosylation.
source: Analysis of the FlaB0 sequence revealed that these five amino acids were all within a N-X-S/T sequon (Figure 6F), a highly conserved consensus sequence for N-linked glycosylation (Jarrell et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The remaining asparagine residues in FlaB0 were not part of a N-X-S/T sequon and did not show similar densities nearby.
source: Consistent with this finding, the remaining asparagine residues were not part of such a sequon and did not show a similar density nearby.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as a consistency check.

claim: No densities were observed adjacent to serine, threonine, proline or lysine sidechains in FlaB0, suggesting that O-linked glycosylation is not present in the Pyrococcus furiosus archaellum.
source: Furthermore, no such densities were observed adjacent to serine, threonine, proline or lysine sidechains, suggesting that O-linked glycosylation is not present in the P. furiosus archaellum.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as an inference from the absence of densities.

claim: Due to the flexibility of glycan chains, only the densities of the first one or two sugar subunits were present in the Pyrococcus furiosus archaellum map.
source: Due to the flexibility of glycan chains, only the densities of the first one or two sugar subunits were present in our map.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text as an explanation for the limited glycan density.

claim: The N-glycosylation sites in FlaB0 are evenly distributed over the exposed part of the peptide.
source: The N-glycosylation sites are evenly distributed over the exposed part of the iFlaB0 peptide (Figure 6D), thus creating a homogeneous, highly glycosylated surface that covers the entire filament (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by reference to figures.

claim: The universal sequence of the Pyrococcus furiosus N-glycan has been determined previously by mass spectrometry.
source: The universal sequence of the P. furiosus N-glycan has been determined previously by mass spectrometry (Fujinami et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Glycosylation adds a substantial mass to each FlaB0 monomeric unit and covers most of the filament surface.
